title: Stories and Prayers of St. Nicholas
subtitle: Selected episodes from the Life and a prayer for sailors
source: Stories drawn from common Synaxaria of the 4th-9th centuries. The troparion is the standard Byzantine Greek hymn for his feast, public-domain English translation. Marginal notes by the editors of Purify.

sections.title: The three bags of gold
paragraphs: In the town of Patara, while Nicholas was still a young deacon, lived a man who had once been rich and was now ruined. He had three daughters and no dowry for any of them. Their marriages were impossible, and he was preparing to sell them into shame in order to feed them.

Nicholas heard of it. He took a leather purse, filled it with the gold his parents had left him, and that night dropped it in secret through a window of the man's house. The eldest was married the next month. The middle daughter's turn came; again at night a second purse arrived through the window. By the third night the father was watching, and when Nicholas threw the third purse and turned to run, the man chased him into the street and caught him by the cloak.

He fell at the deacon's feet, weeping, and called him father, savior, and friend. Nicholas told him to say nothing of it while he lived. The Synaxarion has not kept his name. It has kept what he did: three poor daughters spared the wages of poverty by a gift no one asked them to repay.
notes: The three bags of gold, distilled into folklore over a thousand years, are the seed of every later legend of gifts that arrive at night in winter. The Orthodox memory keeps the original sharper: this was almsgiving against trafficking, given by a priest who refused to be thanked.
Patara is on the southern coast of modern Turkey. The ruins of its harbor and basilica can still be visited.

sections.title: Troparion of St. Nicholas
paragraphs: The hymn that is sung at every Liturgy of St. Nicholas, in every Orthodox church in the world, on the sixth of December:

A rule of faith and an image of meekness, a teacher of self-control hath thy humility shown thee to be unto thy flock. Therefore hast thou achieved high things by thy lowliness, and riches by thy poverty. O father and hierarch Nicholas, intercede with Christ God that our souls may be saved.

The hymn does not mention the wonders, the storms calmed, the prisoners delivered, the dead raised. It says only: rule of faith, image of meekness, teacher of self-control. The wonders rest on the man. The man rests on Christ.
notes: The troparion is the standard hymn for any saint commemorated at Liturgy. Each saint has his own; their texts are among the densest theology the Church sings.

The phrase 'rule of faith' (kanon pisteos) was used by Irenaeus and the early Fathers for the apostolic confession against the Gnostics. Applying it to a bishop of the third century is no small praise.
